newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France's LVMH tangled in DFS bid row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France's LVMH tangled in DFS bid row.

text.p: Bernard Arnault, one of France's leading businessmen who controls luxury goods flagship LVMH, on Friday became entangled in a row between the U.S. owners of DFS and risked a stand-off with Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co (KKR).

Shares of leather goods-to-cognac and champagne group LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton fell sharply in the morning on the Paris Bourse on fears, prompted by an article in the Wall Street Journal, that KKR could mount a rival bid to LVMH for DFS Group Ltd of San Francisco, one of the world's leading duty-free retailers.

The possibility of a bidding war between a top French entrepreneur and financial wizard against the KKR investment house that won tobacco group R.J.R Nabisco in the late 1980s did not reassure investors and LVMH fell in a rising market.
But information from the Arnault camp later in the day, saying a KKR bid was conditional upon LVMH dropping its deal, calmed spirits and steadied LVMH's shares, a dealer said.
LVMH agreed in October to buy a majority stake in DFS for 12.6 billion francs ($2.5 billion) in order to extend its reach in the prosperous south east Asia and Pacific Rim regions.
That deal was with two of the group's four controlling shareholders, Charles Feeny and Alan M. Parker.
But the transaction angered billionaire Robert Miller, a 38.75 percent DFS owner, and fourth stakeholder Anthony Pilaro.

Miller and Pilaro contend that Feeny and Parker went against a 1991 shareholders pact in agreeing to sell their stake to LVMH. The Miller camp has asked a mediator to arbitrate and have requested the commercial court in New York to suspend the LVMH deal until a solution is found.
DFS caters to the same group of affluent customers who buy Louis Vuitton leather goods and designer luggage, Christian Dior perfumes, Hennessy cognacs and Moet & Chandon champagnes.

Even before the confusion has cleared in the row between the shareholders of one of the world's leading empires of duty-free sales, one of Wall Street's sharpest financial boutiques is preparing its moves.
The Wall Street Journal said that KKR has told all four controlling DFS shareholders that it was willing to make a bid, without detailing its possible financial commitments.
In Paris, a source close to LVMH said this offer, contained in a letter which she had seen, was conditional upon the LVMH deal being dropped.
"The Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co initiative is conditional on LVMH and the vendors renouncing their contract of the first of October 1996," she said.
"But the sellers and LVMH have let it be known that they have no intention of doing so," she added.
DFS has more than 15 billion francs in sales from 180 shops and has more than 20 years' experience in retailing in Asia, LVMH said last month. ($ = 5.089 French Francs)
